result.summary: I've treated ticket R/13 as a safety emergency and handed it to the team at high priority. Mr Finch is 84, lives alone and has a heart condition. He has had no heating or hot water since 6 Oct, it is near freezing overnight, and he now says he feels dizzy. The landlord hasn't replied to three emails and is away until 20 Oct. Emergency safety work doesn't need the landlord's approval, but there is no contractor on record for me to assign. So the team needs to phone Mr Finch to check on him and send an emergency engineer. I texted Mr Finch with health and keep-warm advice, texted the landlord, recorded both people's details on file, moved the ticket forward and set a follow-up for 6 hours.
result.situation: At 6 Primrose Court, Mr Finch (84, heart condition, walking frame, lives alone) has had no heating or hot water since 6 Oct. The boiler display is blank and 3C was forecast overnight. The landlord was emailed for approval of up to £200 on 6 Oct and chased on 7 and 8 Oct with no reply. Their out-of-office says they are away until 20 Oct. The 48-hour approval timer ran out on 8 Oct, but no engineer was sent. On 9 Oct Mr Finch texted that the heating is still off, he is wearing his coat indoors and he feels dizzy.

judgement.why_this_decision: Under the emergency rule, no heating for a vulnerable tenant in cold weather is an emergency. Mr Finch is 84 with a heart condition (event 001), the landlord hasn't replied in two days and is away until 20 Oct (event 005), and he now feels dizzy (event 006). Approval doesn't hold up emergency safety work, but there is no contractor on record to assign, and checking on his welfare needs a person on the phone. So I escalated at high priority, gave safe advice and told the landlord.
